candidates.title: Terry, The Shanty Book, Part I: Sailor Shanties (1921), Project Gutenberg #20774
candidates.quote: The song was rendered by one singer, called the shantyman, and the chorus by the sailors
candidates.reason: Primary shanty collection whose editor gives his own account of performance: one singer leads, the crew answers, and the shantyman improvises topical and sarcastic verses.
candidates.supports: song leader and crew response; occupational repertory (shanty); improvised verses; complaint and satire inside work song

candidates.title: Sharp, English Folk-Chanteys, with pianoforte accompaniment, introduction and notes (1914), Internet Archive djvu text
candidates.quote: by assuring unanimity of action, to aid them in the efficient execution of their collective task
candidates.reason: Primary collection; Sharp defines the chantey by its function — unanimity of action for the collective task — and separates capstan (continuous) from pulling (spasmodic) chanties.
candidates.supports: fit of rhythm to a task (hauling, capstan work); occupational repertory (shanty); song leader and crew response

candidates.title: Allen, Ware and Garrison, Slave Songs of the United States (1867), Internet Archive djvu text
candidates.quote: two measures are to be sung to each stroke, the first measure being accented by the beginning of the stroke
candidates.reason: Primary 1867 anthology; the collectors' note gives the rowing-song measure-to-stroke correspondence and the stroke rate, and names the songs used for heavy loads or contrary tide.
candidates.supports: fit of rhythm to a task (rowing); field and boat work repertory; song leader and crew response

candidates.title: Bücher, Arbeit und Rhythmus (Leipzig, 1896), Internet Archive djvu text
candidates.quote: es ist kein Zweifel, dass das Festhalten eines gleichen Zeitmasses der Bewegung dadurch erleichtert wird
candidates.reason: Primary theoretical monograph of the labour-and-rhythm thesis: the sound that marks the stroke falls at the end of the work movement and makes an even time-measure easier to hold; examples run smith, locksmith, tinsmith, cooper, carpenter, shoemaker, weaver.
candidates.supports: fit of rhythm to a task (pounding, craft work); the design principle that song rhythm is derived from the tool's stroke

candidates.title: Collinson, The Oyster Dredging Songs of the Firth of Forth, Scottish Studies 5 (1961)
candidates.quote: They were said to be chanted by a song-leader among the boat’s crew, who repeated his lines in chorus
candidates.reason: Peer-reviewed field study of a single occupational repertory: words always improvised, chanted by a song-leader and repeated in chorus, sung only when wind failed; informants also describe the last two men who knew the song.
candidates.supports: song leader and crew response; improvised verses; occupational repertory; how a work song is learned, owned and retired

candidates.title: Blankenhorn, A New Approach to the Classification of Gaelic Song, Oral Tradition 32/1 (2018) 71-140
candidates.quote: Waulking-songs are work songs performed to facilitate the fulling of handwoven woolen cloth
candidates.reason: Peer-reviewed classification essay that treats work context, not theme, as the classifier of Gaelic song; lists waulking, rowing, harvest and quern songs under Songs of Labour and records that rowing songs survive inside the waulking repertory.
candidates.supports: occupational repertories (waulking, rowing, harvest, quern); fit of rhythm to a task; repertory migration when the task dies

candidates.title: Bourke, Working and Weeping: Women's Oral Poetry in Irish and Scottish Gaelic (UCD, 1988)
candidates.quote: a work song helps the people who sing it to establish the rhythm of their work and to coordinate their effort
candidates.reason: Scholarly essay (open repository) that states the general function of work song — rhythm, coordinated effort and breathing, solidarity — and compares waulking songs with sea shanties and chain-gang songs.
candidates.supports: fit of rhythm to a task; song leader and crew response; solidarity function

candidates.title: Purser, Hebridean Rowing Songs, Angles 17 (2024)
candidates.quote: Rowing songs survive in the Scottish Gaelic tradition in some numbers, but they are no longer in use
candidates.reason: Peer-reviewed article on the iorram: the term covers boat songs and other rhythmic work songs, rowing songs survive as waulking songs after rowing ceased, and the article quotes Blankenhorn's formal profile (call and response, strong regular rhythm, refrains).
candidates.supports: fit of rhythm to a task (rowing); occupational repertory; how a work song is retired and reused

candidates.title: Whall, Ships, Sea Songs and Shanties (Glasgow, 1913), Internet Archive djvu text
candidates.quote: one mariner sings out and the rest follow in the same tune
candidates.reason: Primary collection by a master mariner; glosses the 1450 Complaynt of Scotland anchor-hauling shanty as one mariner singing out and the rest following, the earliest English description of the leader/response hauling song.
candidates.supports: song leader and crew response; occupational repertory (shanty); hauling

candidates.title: SIL Philippines, Mangali and Tanudan Valley Music (field documentation, Kalinga)
candidates.quote: Tug-om is sung by women while pounding rice or coffee.
candidates.reason: Institutional field documentation listing Kalinga song categories by the task they accompany: tug-om for pounding rice or coffee, suggi yaw for harvest cutting and hauling.
candidates.supports: fit of rhythm to a task (pounding); field-work repertory outside the Atlantic
